evals.prompt: I'm the first partnerships hire at Meridian Stack - B2B SaaS, about 140 people, three product lines (a data-quality product, an observability product, and a compliance-reporting add-on we launched in March). My VP wants a partner ecosystem map for the whole company by the end of the month. I've pulled the raw material together already: 34 companies that emailed our partnerships@ alias over the past year asking to partner, plus 11 agencies and consultancies I know personally from my last job. Can you turn that into the map? ARR is about $18M, mid-market ICP, sales-led with a self-serve entry tier.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to map all three product lines at once, a scoping choice offered back to the user, rejection of the inbound-request and personal-network list as an inventory source, a redirect to the internal data pull as the first evidence source, and the remaining interview questions - not a finished map.
expectations: Refuses to map all three product lines at once and states the one-business-area scoping rule.
Offers the named product lines as two or three candidate scopes and waits for the user to choose rather than picking one silently.
Names the inbound partnerships@ list and the personally-known agencies as an invalid source for the inventory rather than accepting them as the starting list.
Gives the reason: teams that build inventories that way sign partners with no shared accounts, no shared ICP, and no path to joint pipeline.
Directs the inventory to be rebuilt from customer and CRM evidence instead.
Names the internal data pull - CRM records, closed-won notes, support tickets, integration and product usage - as the evidence source to start with.
Justifies starting there on the ground that every name it returns is evidence the player touched a real customer.
Keeps the 34 inbound companies only as unverified candidates to check against customer evidence, never as inventory.
Asks what decision is waiting on the map and by what date.
Asks whether this is a one-off executive ask or a compounding asset.
Asks the effort ceiling: the user's own hours, whose calendars they can command, how much political capital they can spend.
Does not produce a finished ecosystem map, classification, or prioritization in this reply.

evals.prompt: Rowanbridge Analytics - B2B SaaS for hospital finance teams, about 9M in ARR, 60 staff. I am the entire partnerships function: one person, no budget, and I can't get an hour on anyone else's calendar until Q3 because the exec team froze all internal meetings during the funding round. I need the partner landscape for our revenue-cycle product in roughly three weeks. Also worth knowing: I work from a locked-down laptop with no internet access at all, so anything outside our own systems and my own phone calls is off the table. Where do I get the raw material from, and in what order?
evals.expected_output: An evidence-source ordering stated explicitly, with the workshop and the public sweep both deleted for this user's stated constraints and named as deleted, the internal data pull recommended as the default, and customer interviews named as the escalation with its trigger.
expectations: Names the internal data pull as the default and the place to start.
States the ordering of evidence sources out loud rather than leaving it implied by the order of a list.
Separates effort from value rather than collapsing them into one blended ranking.
States that the internal data pull and the public sweep tie on effort: each is an hour or two of one person, needing nobody's permission and no calendar.
States that they do not tie on value, and that the internal data pull wins that axis because only its output is evidence about this company's own customers.
Deletes the Value Network Analysis participative workshop because the user's effort ceiling is solo, and says explicitly that it is deleted rather than merely ranking it last.
Gives the reason the workshop is deleted: it needs other people to say yes.
Deletes the public sweep because the user cannot browse the web, and says so rather than listing a source nobody can reach.
Does not recommend competitor partner directories, marketplace listings, review-site category neighbours, or conference sponsor lists to this user.
Names customer interviews as the escalation and gives the trigger: closed-won notes naming third parties that cannot be classified, or an empty influence band.
States that an empty influence band is a gap in the company's own logging rather than evidence the ecosystem has no influencers.
Does not put the workshop first on the strength of its value alone.

evals.prompt: Calderwood Systems, B2B SaaS, workforce scheduling for logistics companies, $24M ARR. The ecosystem map for our EU business goes in front of the board on 3 December, so about three weeks out. One of our integration partners, Fenwick Logistics Cloud, has verbally agreed to swap filtered account lists with us. Our legal team quotes six weeks minimum for any data-sharing agreement plus a privacy review, and nobody else has agreed to share anything yet. I'd much rather have real account-level overlap numbers than guesses - how do I get them in time?
evals.expected_output: The interview-and-tech-stack proxy recommended as the mechanic for this map, account mapping deleted with its reason recorded rather than parked as phase two, the compliance-cost axis surfaced separately, and an explicit ban on the board deliverable claiming account-level overlap it did not measure.
expectations: Recommends the interview-and-tech-stack proxy as the overlap mechanic for this first map.
States plainly that the proxy is directional per category and never per account.
States that permissioned account mapping is the only mechanic that yields overlap at account granularity.
Deletes account mapping for this map because the privacy review will not clear inside the three-week window.
Records the deletion together with its reason rather than carrying account mapping as a phase-two item.
Gives the reason for that rule: a mechanic parked as phase two is how a map ships claiming account-level overlap it never measured.
Surfaces compliance cost as its own axis, naming the data-sharing agreement, the privacy review, and an account list that cannot be un-shared once sent.
States that account mapping only overtakes the proxy on efficiency once three or more partners will share, because the legal and filtering setup is paid once and reused per partner.
Notes that only one partner has agreed here, which keeps the proxy ahead on efficiency.
Does not let the absence of account mapping stall or postpone the exercise.
Requires overlap to be approximated from evidence - what customers say they use and buy through - never from assumption.
States that the board deliverable must not present account-level overlap figures it did not measure.

evals.prompt: Here's my player list for Ostara Cloud's identity product (B2B, enterprise, roughly $40M ARR). Classify each one, one label each, so I can drop it straight into a spreadsheet column. Halbrook IT - resells our licences turnkey with a bit of config, no ongoing contract. Stenning Group - runs our product for 40 client hospitals on a monthly retainer, and also resells licences to them. Verrick Partners - builds custom identity architectures across four vendors including us, big enterprise projects. AWS Marketplace - about 15% of our new bookings flow through it. Dunmore Labs - they built an integration into their HR suite and ship it to their own customers. I also deliberately left Caskett Identity and two other competitors off the list since they aren't partners. Give me the single cleanest label for each so the map stays readable.
evals.expected_output: A two-axis classification rather than one label per player, hybrid roles recorded as hybrid, the MSP/VAR and SI/VAR boundaries drawn on the stated criteria, the marketplace kept on the map as a route to market, and the excluded competitors put back.
expectations: Classifies each player on two axes - role in the customer journey and engagement depth - rather than assigning one label.
Names the journey-role axis as influence, transact, or integrate-and-deliver.
Attributes the trifurcation of the channel to Jay McBain (Canalys).
Names the engagement-depth rungs: listing, integration, co-marketing, co-selling, embedded.
Refuses the single-cleanest-label request for the players carrying more than one role and records hybrid roles as hybrid.
Records Stenning Group as carrying both an MSP role and a reseller role rather than picking one.
Distinguishes MSP from reseller/VAR by contract duration rather than by activity.
Classifies Halbrook IT as a reseller/VAR that resells turnkey with additions and Verrick Partners as an SI that builds new custom solutions, stating that distinction.
Treats AWS Marketplace as a route to market rather than a partner per se, while keeping it on the map because it transacts and influences.
Puts the excluded competitors back on the map and states that coopetition, and the partners shared with competitors, is signal rather than noise.
Does not rank or score the engagement-depth rungs against each other.
Does not recommend moving any named player up the depth ladder as an output of this classification step.
States that a forced single label is a misclassification that misroutes enablement and compensation.

evals.prompt: Thornhill Data, B2B SaaS, $31M ARR. I have four ecosystem categories and last quarter's partner-sourced revenue for each. Rank them so I know where next year's partner budget goes, and use one 5-point scorecard across all four so the comparison stays fair. Referral/affiliate band: $410K sourced last quarter, dirt cheap to run, 31 partners. ISV/integration partners: $95K sourced, but integrations came up in a lot of our closed-won notes and our API already shipped - no partner manager assigned to them though. Regional SIs: $0 sourced, the enterprise segment is basically uncovered for us, and we have no implementation docs. Cloud marketplace listing: $60K sourced, buyers in our segment mostly aren't procuring there yet. Rank by revenue contribution and tell me the budget split.
evals.expected_output: A refusal of both the single shared scorecard and the revenue-first ranking, the four categories placed on the strategic-fit x ease-of-execution 2x2 with the quadrant order stated, and the two out-of-scope ranking questions handed off by name.
expectations: Refuses the single shared scorecard and requires scorecard weights segmented by partner type.
Gives the reason: each partner type has a different route to revenue, cycle length, and influence.
Rejects ranking by last quarter's partner-sourced revenue as over-weighting a lagging indicator.
States that over-weighting lagging revenue is the most-cited error the scorecard exists to prevent, and that here it would rank the referral band first and the ISVs last.
Plots the four categories on a strategic fit x ease of execution 2x2 instead of a single revenue ranking.
Attributes the partnerships-specific 2x2 to Chris Lavoie.
Names the four quadrants: holy grail, next best choice, uphill battle, low priority.
States the resulting order out loud: holy grail > next best choice > uphill battle > low priority.
Places the ISV/integration category in the holy grail quadrant, citing the closed-won evidence and the shipped API.
Names the missing partner manager as the capacity gap to fix, and puts capacity to support a category inside its prioritization score rather than treating it as an afterthought.
Places the referral/affiliate band in next best choice and states plainly that cheap to run is not the same as high priority.
Places the cloud marketplace listing in low priority because buyers are not procuring there yet, with a re-score trigger when procurement behaviour shifts.

Hands sequencing of categories the company does not yet run to mbfinotti/partnerships-skills@partner-ecosystem-expansion, and ranking of named candidate companies to mbfinotti/partnerships-skills@alliance-prioritization.

evals.prompt: Kestrel Freight Systems, B2B SaaS for freight brokers, $12M ARR. I've finished scoring six partner categories on our weighted scorecard - composites came out between 2.1 and 4.3. Next thing I want is the Ideal Partner Profile written up. Just take our ICP (freight brokers, 50-500 employees, US and Canada, running a TMS) and use that as the IPP so recruiting knows what to look for. One IPP for the whole program is fine, we're small.
evals.expected_output: A correction that the IPP is not the ICP copied across, one IPP per surviving category rather than one program-wide, and the JVP kill test relocated ahead of scoring with a retro-run on the six already-scored categories.
expectations: States that the Ideal Partner Profile is not the ICP copied across.
Defines the IPP as a profile of the company best placed to bring you those customers, not a profile of the customer.
Refuses a single program-wide IPP and requires one IPP per partner category that survives prioritization.
Names the IPP as an output of the map rather than an input to it.
Names the IPP criteria families: firmographics, customer-base overlap with the ICP, delivery capability, economic motivation, and solution fit or sales-motion alignment.
States that the Joint Value Proposition workshop belongs before scoring, not after it.
States that a category which cannot articulate joint customer value does not proceed.
Gives the reason for that ordering: a category that fails the test never receives a composite that later has to be retracted.
Recommends retro-running the JVP test across the six already-scored categories and retracting the composite of any that fail.

Names at least three of the JVP workshop questions, drawn from the fundamental customer benefit, each side's differentiated contribution, how the offerings combine, the customer-visible outcome, why a customer should trust the pairing, and who the target is.
Names the WIIFT question explicitly - whether the partner category's own motivation is obvious.
States that a weak JVP combined with high overlap is the uphill-battle quadrant, feeding the verdict back into the 2x2.

evals.prompt: Ambervale Robotics - industrial automation, B2B, we sell through distributors and systems integrators. Board deck goes out on the 14th. I want a proper network diagram of the whole partner ecosystem, plus the concentric-circle tier view showing who our gold, silver and bronze partners are, plus a heat map, plus the matrix. More views, more credible. Nobody on my team has any design or data-viz skill - I'll be building these in slides myself. The board question is simple: where do we put next year's channel investment?
evals.expected_output: One recommended format rather than four, the matrix recommended for this investment question, the network diagram deleted for lack of layout skill, the tiered view skipped as a restatement of the 2x2, and the concentric-circles-are-not-tiers correction.
expectations: Does not build all four views.
Recommends the matrix as the format for this board question, since the decision in front of the board is where to invest.
States the format ordering out loud rather than leaving it implied by row order.
Describes the matrix as near-zero build because it is a table fed by scorecard composites already computed.
Deletes the network diagram because nobody on the team has layout skill.
States that without layout skill the network diagram reads as a hairball and settles nothing, and does not present it as the ambitious option.
Names the question only the network diagram can answer - who the hubs are - and the condition that would promote it: a hub decision plus someone with real layout skill free.
Skips the tiered view because the prioritization 2x2 already carries that ranking.
Gives the reason: two views of one ranking invite the reader to look for a difference that is not there.
Corrects the premise that the concentric circles show gold, silver and bronze tiers, stating the circles are a map layout and must not be presented as tier criteria.
Points tier criteria and benefits to mbfinotti/partnerships-skills@partner-tiering rather than producing them here.
Names the heat map as what to build instead when the stated goal is coverage gaps rather than investment, and notes it needs one clean dimension attached to every player.

evals.prompt: Loxley Grid, B2B SaaS, energy-sector analytics, $27M ARR. Our partner count went from 60 to 180 over 18 months. 22 of them registered a deal in the last 90 days. Our CRM has one field called 'Partner Involved' - a checkbox - and nothing that separates sourced from influenced, and IT has a hard freeze on new CRM fields until next fiscal year. Two of our categories only hold 5 and 6 partners each. Somebody on the exec team keeps repeating that partners drive 28% of revenue at good companies and asking why we're not there. Give me the health read on this ecosystem.
evals.expected_output: The activation ratio read first and computed, the recruitment-outrunning-enablement diagnosis, the sourced-versus-influenced split deleted with the earning question declared unanswered rather than pending, and every quoted benchmark carrying a provenance flag.
expectations: Reads the activation ratio first and computes it from the given numbers: 22 of 180, roughly 12%.
States why it is read first: it is one query and it invalidates a whole class of map.
Diagnoses partner count tripling while activation stays low as recruitment running ahead of enablement.
States that the map should flag that category rather than celebrate its size.
Names logo collecting explicitly, and that a partner list is not a channel.
Deletes the sourced-versus-influenced split because the CRM cannot carry those fields in the time available.
Says plainly that the earning question - whether the ecosystem makes money at all - stays unanswered, rather than carrying it as a pending metric.
Gives the reason: carrying it as pending lets a later reader assume it was measured.
States that sourced and influenced must never be summed without a written overlap policy, and that a single 'Partner Involved' checkbox cannot separate them.
Tracks the two categories holding 5 and 6 partners as raw counts rather than percentages, because below roughly eight partners one partner going quiet swings a rate by double digits.
Flags the 28% figure with its provenance as analyst and secondhand rather than repeating it as established fact.

States that partner-sourced revenue share is category-dependent and never transferable across categories, contrasting the SaaS median near 24% with hardware and security near 41% and services-led near 58%.
States that the company's own baseline tracked by cohort beats any external benchmark.
Declines to offer a single comparable industry benchmark for partner-influenced revenue share, stating that definitions of influenced differ per company so the figures are not comparable.

evals.prompt: Fenmarsh Outdoor - we make hiking and camping gear, sell through about 400 independent retailers plus three national chains, and our own webstore has gone from 8% to 26% of revenue in two years. Three of our biggest retail accounts have now formally complained about our direct discounting and one threatened to cut our shelf facings in half. Map our partner ecosystem and give me the rules we should put in place so this stops. Also, everything I read about partner ecosystems is B2B SaaS - does any of this even apply to a gear brand?
evals.expected_output: The D2C-versus-retail conflict detected and sized but not resolved, rules of engagement handed off by name, the levers listed as observed practice and left unranked with a stated reason, and an explicit answer that the method's spine is identical in B2B and B2C with the four dimensions that genuinely change.
expectations: Detects and sizes the D2C-versus-retail conflict but does not write the rules of engagement.
Hands the rules of engagement to mbfinotti/partnerships-skills@partner-channel-conflict by name.
Quantifies the conflict zone by accounts, revenue at stake, and territory.
Names D2C versus retail as the signature B2C conflict, distinct from the partner-versus-partner and direct-versus-partner patterns.
Notes that D2C is resource-intensive and that its payoff is first-party data, margin, and brand control.

Lists the observed levers - channel-exclusive ranges or editions, D2C-priority allocation of high-demand products, selective retention of key retail partners - as observed practice rather than prescription.
Leaves those levers deliberately unranked and says why: the ranking depends on contract terms this exercise never reads.
Answers the B2B/B2C question by stating the method's spine is identical in both rather than reinventing a consumer-side method.

Names what stays identical, including the identify-analyze-visualize-optimize sequence, the one-business-area scoping rule, the map-from-customer-data-not-inbound-requests rule, the recurring-review discipline, and strategic-fit x ease-of-execution prioritization.
Names what genuinely changes between B2B and B2C: partner vocabulary, partner counts, attribution, and signature conflict.
Uses B2C partner vocabulary - retail and wholesale, creators and affiliates, licensing, co-branding - rather than resellers, VARs, MSPs and SIs.

Frames B2C attribution as transactional and fast-cycling, comparing lifetime value of partnership-acquired customers against other channels plus brand lift, rather than sourced-versus-influenced pipeline over long cycles.
Flags any quoted figure on pipeline lost to unresolved conflict as vendor-published and directional.

evals.prompt: Done! Here's the ecosystem map for Vantry Commerce's payments product. Six players on it: two payment ISVs, three agencies and one marketplace. Overlap I estimated myself - I know these accounts well enough, it's roughly 40% overlap with the ISVs and maybe 15% with the agencies. It's one slide, colour-coded, looks great. I'm sending it to our CEO on Friday and then we're going to go recruit ten more agencies. Anything you'd add before I send?
evals.expected_output: A plain statement that the map fails the pass threshold, each failed criterion named, an honest next step scoped instead of a polish pass, and the deliverable redirected from one slide to a two-page memo with its mandatory open-questions section.
expectations: States plainly that the map does not pass, rather than polishing or approving it.
Names the player-count failure against the at-least-ten-players threshold.
Names the overlap failure: the 40% and 15% figures are assumption, not account-mapping output or customer-interview evidence.
Names the missing retroactive closed-won influence analysis.
Names the missing decision with an owner, and states that a map driving no decision is the discipline's most common failure.
Names the requirement that every quoted benchmark carry a provenance flag.
Scopes the honest next step - customer interviews and a closed-won deal review - rather than shipping a decorative map.
Warns against recruiting the ten agencies before overlap is verified.
Names the failure this would repeat: signing partners with no shared accounts, no shared ICP, and no path to joint pipeline.
Requires the deliverable be an ecosystem strategy memo of roughly two pages rather than a single colour-coded slide.
Names the open-questions section as mandatory, with the reason that a map with no stated uncertainty is a map that stopped asking.
Requires every memo claim to name its source, contrasting a reviewable claim against an unsourced assertion.
Sets a recurring review cadence plus immediate-update triggers: a merger or acquisition, new regulation, and a category moving quadrants.
